extracted.intended_audience: physicians, surgeons, coroners, and medically informed readers interested in distinguishing life from apparent death
extracted.subtask_description: Clinical/forensic evaluation to distinguish real ( irreversible ) death from states of suspended or minimal vitality (apparent death) using physiological definitions, observations, and provocations of circulation, respiration, and innervation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical definition of life
rubrics_metrics.description: For practical purposes life may be provisionally defined as the continuous individual integration and differentiation of material energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual definition emphasizes that living systems constantly incorporate and transform external materials/energy (integration) while producing organized, differentiated activity. Use this as the conceptual baseline when judging whether observed processes indicate life or mere physical/chemical phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential functions required for life
rubrics_metrics.description: Man's functions may be classified into essential and supplemental — the former including such as cannot be discontinued beyond a brief interval without fatal consequences (circulation, innervation, respiration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete cessation of any one of the essential functions (circulation, innervation, or respiration) must quickly lead to death. Assess these three systems first when deciding between real and apparent death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation as a diagnostic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation is a vital necessity; cardiac contractions are a sine qua non to propel blood and effect mass-motion of the circulatory fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for cardiac contractions (directly or by pulse), movement of blood in accessible capillaries, or signs of active capillary perfusion. If circulation can be artificially excited in an exposed part (see provocation tests), that indicates vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innervation/neurological activity as a diagnostic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Innervation is essential: tissue-elements must retain continuity with the presiding nerve-center so that peripheral impressions may be transmitted and reflected (e.g., vaso-motor reflexes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for nervous-mediated responses (e.g., vaso-motor changes to peripheral stimulation). Absence of innervation-mediated reactions supports death; presence (even minimal) supports potential reversibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration and respiratory-exchange evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Respiratory apparatus eliminates products (notably carbonic acid); the detention of expiratory carbonic acid is evidence of vitality, while its utter absence under adequate tests is undeniable proof of the opposite condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tests for expired CO2 (or other adequate tests of gas exchange) as a sensitive marker: detected exhaled CO2 indicates respiration/life; absence after adequate testing is strong evidence of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between essential and supplemental function loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Some functions (hepatic, renal, even certain organic processes) may be suspended without involving general dissolution, whereas cessation of essential functions is fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate absence of supplemental functions with death. Emphasize checks for essential functions (circulation, innervation, respiration) rather than ancillary processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capillary reaction / cutaneous efflorescence test
rubrics_metrics.description: The cutis vera (superficial vascular tissue) shows excessive accumulation of red corpuscles as a sensible floridity; this reactive redness can be temporarily displaced (blanched) and renewed by recurrent pressure if vital circulation is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply local pressure to accessible skin: vital capillary congestive redness will blanch with pressure and return quickly when pressure is released. This reversible blanching/return is a practical bedside sign of residual circulation and thus vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocative stimulation of circulation in exposed parts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are means of artificially exciting preternatural activity of the circulation in parts open to observation, during minimum degrees of vitality; such provocation affords a reliable method of deciding existence or non-existence of the vital process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local irritants (e.g., heat) or other stimuli on exposed tissues to elicit increased capillary flow or other circulatory responses. A positive provoked response indicates viability even when baseline signs are minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic observation of microcirculation as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing circulation in the web of a frog's foot shows capillary fluctuations (slackening, oscillation, retrograde flow) and marked increase and cohesion of corpuscles after irritant application; analogous capillary phenomena inform human assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, inspect microcirculation (or analogous superficial capillaries) for active motion patterns and responsive changes to stimulation. Such micro-observations can distinguish between living reactive circulation and post-mortem stasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vital versus post-mortem vesication and underlying cutis appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Vital vesication (from heat irritation) yields a fibrino-albuminous solution coagulable by heat and an underlying cutis that retains floridity and renewability; post-mortem vesication contents are generally gaseous or serous, and the underlying cutis is unalterably yellowish-white, crisp, and horny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If vesicles form, assess their contents and the appearance of the underlying cutis after removing the loosely adherent cuticle: coagulable fibrino-albuminous fluid and a florid subjacent cutis indicate vitality; gaseous/serous contents and a yellowish-white crisp cutis indicate post-mortem change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of blood physical characters and corpuscles
rubrics_metrics.description: Human blood is semi-solid with innumerable white and red corpuscles; the absolute number of red corpuscles corresponds with general vitality, and local aggregation (capillary congestion) is observable in vital reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the presence, mobility, and aggregation of red corpuscles in peripheral tissues as supportive evidence. Localized aggregation that changes with stimulation favors vitality; fixed post-mortem congestion does not show such responsive behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use caution to avoid premature burial; require absolute diagnostic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions not incompatible with resuscitation may render functions directly imperceptible; therefore it is important to discover signs absolutely diagnostic of real or apparent death to prevent premature burial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on absence of obvious motion alone. Perform the battery of provocation and sensitive tests (capillary blanch-return, provoked circulation, respiratory gas detection) before declaring death, especially when resuscitation remains possible.
